title: Past time
subtitle: Past simple, past continuous, past perfect, would, used to, be/get used to

rows.person: I / you / he / she / it / we / they
rows.question: **Did** I/you/he/she/it/we/they **play** …?

blocks.intro: Irregular verbs do not take **-ed** in the past simple.
items: Learn the past simple form of irregular verbs.

rows.example: Tom and I **played** a game of chess and he **won**.
**Did** you **collect** stamps when you were younger?
A famous footballer **lived** in our house before we bought it.

rows.use: General truths and facts about the past
The main events in a story
rows.example: The referee **blew** the whistle and Simon **passed** the ball to James, who **ran** towards the goal.

blocks.text: We can also use **did** in past simple statements for emphasis.
blocks.note: 'Why didn't you win your match yesterday?' 'I **did win**. Who told you I didn't?' · We lost 5–0 but at least we **did get** into the final.

rows.use: Actions happening at a particular moment in the past
rows.example: At five o'clock, I **was reading** my new book.
Greg **was living** in London at the time.
When we were young, my brother **was always borrowing** my toys.

rows.use: Actions in progress over a period of time
rows.example: Daniel **was playing** video games all morning yesterday.

rows.use: Two actions in progress at the same time
rows.example: **Were** Ulla and her friends **playing** Monopoly while we **were playing** draughts?
The sun **was shining** and the birds **were singing**. Lisa opened the window and looked out.

blocks.text: When one action in the past interrupts another action in progress, we use the past simple and the past continuous together.
blocks.note: I **was playing** on my computer when it suddenly **crashed**.

blocks.correct: When we were on holiday, we **played** volleyball every day.
blocks.incorrect: When we were on holiday, we **were playing** volleyball every day.

blocks.text: We do not usually use stative verbs in continuous tenses. See Unit 1.

rows.use: Situations and states before the past
rows.example: We'd **lived** next to the gym for a couple of months before I decided to join.

rows.use: Completed actions before a moment in the past
rows.example: I'd already **bought** the computer game when I saw it was cheaper in another shop.

rows.use: Completed actions where the important thing is the result at a moment in the past
rows.example: We didn't feel like playing Scrabble because we **had just finished** a long game of Monopoly.

blocks.intro: There is often little or no difference in meaning between the past perfect simple and the past simple.
items: We'd **lived** next to the gym for a couple of months before I decided to join.
We **lived** next to the gym for a couple of months before I decided to join.

blocks.text: After we have used the past perfect simple once, we often then use the past simple instead of continuing to use the past perfect.
blocks.note: I **had already had** one flying lesson, which **was** great fun, and I **knew** immediately that I **wanted** to get my pilot's licence.

blocks.text: Phrases such as **it was the first / second / etc. time** … are followed by the past perfect simple.
blocks.note: It was the second time I'd **been** on a plane.

rows.person: I / you / he / she / it / we / they
rows.question: **Had** I/you/he/she/it/we/they **been playing** …?

rows.use: Actions continuing up to a moment in the past
rows.example: When you saw us, we **had been running** for six miles — and we still had a mile to go!

rows.use: Actions stopping just before a moment in the past
rows.example: Sarah looked tired because she **had been exercising** all morning.

rows.use: Past habits, particularly for the distant past
rows.example: When I was very young, my grandfather **would take** me to the park to play.

blocks.text: We don't often use **would** in questions or negative statements with this meaning. In negative statements, we can use **would never**.
blocks.note: We **would never play** games together as a family when I was growing up.

rows.statement: I/you/he/she/it/we/they **used to train** three times a week.
rows.negative: I/you/he/she/it/we/they **didn't use to** / **never used to** be so good at football.
rows.question: **Did** I/you/he/she/it/we/they **use to play** hockey here?

rows.use: Past habits and states, particularly for the distant past
rows.example: My mother **used to play** a lot of squash before I was born.

blocks.correct: We **used to have** a house that was right next to the park.
blocks.incorrect: We **would have** a house that was right next to the park.

blocks.text: To talk about a past **state**, we can use **used to**, but **not would**.

rows.use: A situation that is familiar or no longer strange
rows.example: I didn't like **being** the goalkeeper at first but now I'm **used to** it.

blocks.text: When we want to talk about the process of becoming familiar with something, we use **get used to**.
blocks.note: I'm gradually **getting used to** being in a new team.

exercises.title: H · Similar meaning
exercises.instruction: Complete each second sentence using the word given, so that it has a similar meaning to the first. Write between two and five words.

items.prompt:
People walked more fifty years ago than they do now. **would**
Fifty years ago, ___ than they do now.

My parents wouldn't let me stay out late when I was young. **used**
My parents ___ let me stay out late when I was young.

Did you know that Carol played basketball for her country? **to**
Did you know that Carol ___ basketball for her country?

Sending messages around the world instantly is no longer unusual. **got**
We ___ messages around the world instantly.

When he was a teacher, my dad often used to get home quite late. **would**
When he was a teacher, my dad ___ quite late.

Do you think you could learn to live without your mobile phone? **used**
Do you think you could ___ without your mobile phone?

In the past, people wouldn't go as far away on holiday as they do today. **use**
In the past, people ___ as far away on holiday as they do today.

This town has a lot more cinemas than it had in the past. **used**
This town ___ so many cinemas.

exercises.title: I · Extra word
exercises.instruction: Write the extra word in each line.

items.prompt: Childhood **would used** to be quite different from what it is today. Young
people **didn't use not** to have so much leisure time. Today's children may
complain about their schoolwork, but our great-grandparents **would to go**
out to work at a very young age. They had **often been left** school by
the time they were fourteen and **were found** a job. This meant that they
had had little free time for hobbies or leisure activities, especially when
they had been working hard all day. Of course, they **got themselves used**
to working long hours eventually, but it would meant that they had to
grow up very quickly. Today, we **are got used** to having some free time to
do things we enjoy, a luxury people in the past rarely **were had**.
